title: 2025-01-15 - Technical deep dive: Observability & tracing integration (OpenTelemetry)
transcript:
[00:00] Sam Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Sam from Redwood, I think we have Rita from SE and from Nimbus we have Alex, Priya, Marco. Quick intro then we'll jump into observability and OpenTelemetry integration.

[00:30] Alex Morales: Yep hi, Alex here. We're mainly responsible for the inference platform at Nimbus, we've been testing the Redwood Dedicated beta and want to understand token-level tracing and how OTEL fits into our monitoring stack.

[01:00] Rita Cho: Great, today I want to cover three things: 1) what telemetry Redwood emits by default (token-metrics, KV cache hits, batch timings), 2) how to wire OpenTelemetry exporters (jaeger/prometheus/OTLP), and 3) dashboard patterns for latency/cost SLOs. We'll also dig into the performance overhead and best practices.

[01:30] Priya Singh: Quick note — we run on-prem with a VPC peered setup, so anything about metrics shipping and network egress matters. We also need private key handling for traces if they include PII.

[02:00] Rita Cho: Understood. We have a private deployment pattern for that — you can either push metrics to your internal Prometheus or use OTLP over mTLS to your observability plane. We don't require sending raw tokens offsite; token-level metrics are aggregated counts and histograms, not raw content unless you opt-in for debug traces.

[03:00] Sam Patel: To add, for enterprise we ship a reference OTEL config in the private repo — I'll share the link after the call — it has examples for Jaeger, Grafana Loki, and OTLP collector.

[04:00] Alex Morales: Can you be specific about what "token-level metrics" means? We need to calculate exact token cost per request for chargeback.

[06:00] Rita Cho: Sure. Token-level metrics are broken into: requested_tokens, generated_tokens, kv_cache_hits, kv_cache_misses, batching_wait_ms, model_inference_ms. Each is emitted per request ID and aggregated as histograms and counters. We also emit per-model and per-route labels.

[08:00] Priya Singh: Per-request labels sounds like a lot of cardinality — how do you avoid high cardinality in Prometheus?

[10:00] Rita Cho: Good question. We recommend two things: 1) tag only a small set of dimensions (model, route, customer_tier) and use label_drop/label_keep on the OTLP collector; 2) use histograms with exponential buckets for latency and token counts to avoid cardinality explosion. We also support sampled traces — full traces only on 1% by default.

[15:00] Marco Ruiz: About traces — does Redwood correlate trace spans with KV cache hits? We want to see when KV cache is helping latency.

[20:00] Rita Cho: Yes, our runtime emits spans for key phases: request_enqueue, batching, kv_lookup, kv_hit/kV_miss (note: transcription sometimes shows KV as kayvee), model_forward, response_stream. KV lookup spans include a boolean attribute kv_hit: true/false and the size of cached prefix. In Jaeger/Grafana Tempo you can filter for kv_hit=true and compare model_forward durations.

[30:00] Priya Singh: Any numbers: what's the overhead of adding those spans and token-level counters? We can't accept noticeable p99 regressions.

[40:00] Rita Cho: In our internal benchmarks, trace spans at default sampling (1%) add negligible overhead (<1% p95 latency). If you enable full tracing for debug (all requests) we measure roughly 3-6% CPU and ~5-10ms extra tail latency depending on exporter buffering. For token-level counters (aggregated metrics) the impact is tiny — it's mostly counters incremented in the hot path, implemented in C++ runtime with lock-free counters. Worst case on very high QPS you may see slight contention which is why we recommend pushing to a local OTLP collector.

[44:30] Sam Patel: Also, batching interacts with traces — batching wait time is a span. If you enable continuous batching, you will see request_enqueue waiting longer but model_forward amortized over more tokens. We expose batching_wait_ms and batch_size as attributes.

[44:45] Alex Morales: How do quantization and kernel selection affect observability? For example, if we switch to int8 quant, can we still rely on the same perf counters?

[44:55] Rita Cho: Yes, kernel path is a span attribute (kernel_variant: fp16/int8/fused_attention_v2), and timings are recorded per kernel. Quantization can change token throughput a lot, so you’ll see model_forward_ms changes and different CPU/GPU utilization metrics. We emit queue_depth and gpu_util as supplementary metrics if you enable the extended telemetry bundle.

[45:10] Priya Singh: For VPC/private, can we host the OTLP collector in our subnet and point Redwood runtime to it? How about mTLS?

[45:30] Rita Cho: Absolutely. For private deployments we provide an ENV var to configure OTLP endpoint and an option to use mTLS certs. The runtime can authenticate with client certs and the collector uses mutual TLS. We also support proxying through an internal intake gateway. There are sample Helm charts in the private repo.

[46:00] Marco Ruiz: We'd like to build dashboards showing token-cost per feature flag and SLO alerts for cost drift. What are the recommended query patterns?

[47:00] Rita Cho: Typical dashboards have panels for: tokens_per_second (sum of requested+generated), cost_per_token (multiply by pricing label), p50/p95/p99 model_forward_ms by model and route, kv_cache_hit_ratio (kv_cache_hits / (kv_cache_hits + kv_cache_misses)), and batching_effectiveness (median batch_size and batching_wait_ms). For cost drift, we emit per-route token histograms; you can create an alert on a weekly rolling average of tokens_per_request exceeding a threshold.

[48:00] Alex Morales: Any gotchas for correlating logs and traces? Our SREs want to link errors to request IDs.

[49:00] Rita Cho: We propagate a request_id header through the runtime and include it as trace_id and a log attribute. For private deployments you can forward runtime logs to your Loki stack; the runtime supports structured JSON logs with request_id, model, route, and span_ids.

[50:30] Priya Singh: You mentioned debug traces that include token contents if we opt-in. We require PII controls. How is that gated?

[51:00] Rita Cho: Debug traces are opt-in at the deployment or route level and require an explicit flag. They are always stored locally in private deployments and are encrypted at rest. For hosted customers, we have a compliance process and auditing before enabling raw-token traces. We can also pseudonymize tokens in traces if needed.

[52:00] Sam Patel: I'll note that for Nimbus we should default to aggregated token metrics and sampled traces to avoid PII exposure and cardinality issues.

[53:00] Alex Morales: For our benchmarking—can Redwood run a KV-cache warmup script and produce a report showing cache hit ratios and token-cost savings?

[54:00] Rita Cho: Yes, we have a benchmark harness. We can run a KV warmup scenario and produce CSV with per-run metrics: start_time, requests, kv_hits, kv_misses, average_batch_size, avg_latency_ms. We'll share the spreadsheet (example link: https://drive.google.com/example-benchmark).

[55:00] Marco Ruiz: How do you handle sampling policies? We want higher sampling on errors and anomalies.

[56:00] Rita Cho: You can configure dynamic sampling in the OTLP collector or in our runtime. Rules like: sample 100% on status_code>=500 or response_time>2s; otherwise 1%. We also support probabilistic sampling with rate limits.

[57:00] Priya Singh: Will enabling token-level histograms blow up storage for metrics?

[58:00] Rita Cho: If you use histograms with reasonable bucket counts (e.g., 10-20 buckets) and aggregate at model+route level you should be fine. High-cardinality labels is the primary risk. Use label_rollup for per-customer views if needed.

[59:00] Sam Patel: Quick note on dashboards: Redwood Console exports prebuilt Grafana dashboards you can import; they map to the metrics we emit. I'll drop links.

[59:30] Alex Morales: One more: can we see token-level traces tied to function/tool calls (we use tool-calling heavily)?

[60:00] Rita Cho: Yes, function/tool calls are emitted as child spans with attributes tool_name and tool_latency_ms. You can trace across those spans to see end-to-end latency including external tool calls. For privacy we don't record tool payloads unless explicitly enabled.

[61:00] Marco Ruiz: Security/compliance - will enabling OTEL affect our SOC/ISO posture? We need audit logs of changes to sampling/pipeline.

[62:00] Rita Cho: Audit logs for configuration changes are part of our enterprise package. Changes to sampling and telemetry pipeline are logged with actor, timestamp, and previous_state. We can integrate those logs into your SIEM.

[63:00] Priya Singh: Operational question: if we have a big spike and the OTLP collector is overwhelmed, does the runtime block or drop telemetry?

[64:00] Rita Cho: By default telemetry is buffered asynchronously and will drop on overload, not block the inference path. There are backpressure knobs: you can configure the internal buffer sizes and add local sink to disk for post-facto shipping. We generally recommend sizing the collector or enabling a local sidecar to smooth spikes.

[65:00] Sam Patel: Let's recap real quick — next steps we talked about were: share OTEL config and Grafana dashboards, run a KV warmup benchmark, and schedule a follow-up to review the benchmark and dashboard.

[66:00] Alex Morales: Sounds good. Also please include sample Prometheus queries for kv_cache_hit_ratio and cost per route.

[67:00] Rita Cho: Will do — sample promql: rate(redwood_kv_cache_hits_total[5m]) / (rate(redwood_kv_cache_hits_total[5m]) + rate(redwood_kv_cache_misses_total[5m])) as kv_cache_hit_ratio; and cost_per_route = sum by(route) (rate(redwood_tokens_generated_total[5m]) * label_replace(redwood_pricing_token_usd, "", "$1", "model", "(.*)")) — we'll refine before sending.

[68:00] Marco Ruiz: One logistics item: can you send us the private helm charts and mTLS examples?

[69:00] Sam Patel: Yep I'll share the private repo access request and drop the helm charts.

[70:00] Priya Singh: And timeline — we want to start a pilot next quarter, ideally with Dedicated capacity.

[71:00] Rita Cho: That fits our usual flow — pilot + benchmark + config tweaks. We'll aim to deliver the benchmark run and initial dashboards within two weeks after repo access.

[72:00] Sam Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

[72:10] (recording ends)

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription errors and occasional mis-capitalization, speakers sometimes overlap. Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.ai/docs/observability (reference), private repo helm charts (link shared after call), example benchmark spreadsheet (drive link).
